soil-fert-019.title: What heavy fertilizing does to life underground
soil-fert-019.text: Heavy fertilizer use, especially beyond plant needs, can break down the symbiosis between plant roots and mycorrhizal fungi. Organic and organic–mineral fertilizers increase the abundance of soil animals, while mineral fertilizers do not. Chemical fertilizers boost microbial growth without changing its diversity. Acid stress combined with high nitrogen, rare before industrial agriculture, weakens the links between the aboveground and belowground parts of farm ecosystems. Nitrogen deposition is even turning Sphagnum bogs from stores of carbon into sources of it, by stimulating decomposers. How fertilizers affect soil animals is still debated, since group-specific responses mask the overall effect.

soil-fert-020.title: The climate cost of nitrogen fertilizer
soil-fert-020.text: Around 5% of human greenhouse gas emissions come from making and using nitrogen fertilizer. The gases are carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. About one third comes from production and two thirds from use in the field. Soil bacteria convert nitrate to nitrous oxide, the third most important greenhouse gas. Per ton it is 296 times stronger than carbon dioxide, and it also contributes to ozone depletion. Human nitrous oxide emissions, mostly from fertilizer, came to an estimated 700 million tons of CO2 equivalent between 2007 and 2016. Ammonium-based fertilizers also increase methane emissions from crop fields, notably rice paddies.

soil-fert-006.title: Micronutrient fertilizers: tiny doses, outsized effects
soil-fert-006.text: Some plant nutrients occur in tissue at just 0.15 to 400 ppm, less than 0.04% of dry matter. Yet as enzyme co-factors, their impact far exceeds their concentration. Micronutrient fertilizers supply these elements, typically boron, zinc, molybdenum, iron and manganese, as water-soluble salts. Iron is often given as a chelate such as EDTA or EDDHA, because at moderate pH and phosphate it turns insoluble. Needs depend on plant and setting. Sugar beets need boron and legumes cobalt, while heat or drought makes boron less available. Zinc deficiency is common in soils worldwide, affecting plants and people alike, and zinc fertilizers are widely used against it.

soil-fert-005.title: Reading the three numbers on a fertilizer bag
soil-fert-005.text: A bag marked 10-10-10 carries three promises. The NPK rating is a label of three numbers, separated by dashes, giving a fertilizer's content of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. They are percentages of nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O. Yet the fertilizer contains no actual P2O5 or K2O; the oxides are a conventional shorthand for its phosphorus and potassium. A 50-pound (23 kg) bag labeled 16-4-8 therefore holds 8 lb (3.6 kg) of nitrogen, phosphorus equal to 2 lb of P2O5, and 4 lb of K2O. Australia adds a fourth number, for sulfur, and gives elemental values for all nutrients.

soil-fert-071.title: Ammonium nitrate, stable nitrogen with a dangerous edge
soil-fert-071.text: The salt that feeds a wheat field can, mixed with fuel, become an explosive. Ammonium nitrate is a salt of ammonium and nitrate ions and an important nitrogen fertilizer, with an NPK rating of 34-0-0. It is less concentrated than urea, at 46-0-0, but more stable, and it does not rapidly lose nitrogen to the atmosphere. Factories make it by reacting ammonia from the Haber process with nitric acid. Natural deposits in Chile's Atacama Desert were mined until the Haber–Bosch process made nitrate mining obsolete. Because it forms explosive mixtures with fuels, it is a greater security risk than urea, which is not an oxidizer.

soil-fert-009.title: Potash, named for ashes soaked in a pot
soil-fert-009.text: Before the industrial era, potash was made by soaking plant or wood ashes in water in a pot, which gave it its name. Potash is a mixture of potassium minerals, and potassium fertilizers are made from it. About 90% of potash goes to fertilizer. Potassium is the third major crop nutrient, after nitrogen and phosphorus. The main straight potassium fertilizer is muriate of potash, 95–99% potassium chloride. Others are potassium sulfate, carbonate or nitrate. Labels report potassium as K2O equivalent for comparison, though plants do not take up K2O and the fertilizers contain none.

soil-fert-012.title: Granules or solutions: the two forms of fertilizer
soil-fert-012.text: About 90% of fertilizers reach crops as solids: granules, powders or prills. Urea, diammonium phosphate and potassium chloride are the most common. Liquid fertilizers are water-based solutions of ammonia, ammonium nitrate or urea. Liquids act faster and cover more evenly, while granules are cheaper to ship, store and apply. Dissolving fertilizer in the water piped to crops is called fertigation. It places nutrients where the water goes and allows small doses, reducing fertilizer use and leaching. Growers use it mostly on high-value crops such as vegetables, turf, fruit trees and ornamentals.

soil-fert-018.title: Why foods hold fewer trace minerals than they used to
soil-fert-018.text: Iron, zinc, copper and magnesium concentrations in many foods have fallen over the last 50–60 years. Why is still argued. Intensive farming with synthetic fertilizers is often blamed, and farming without them is often proposed as the remedy. The evidence points mostly elsewhere. Higher yields driven by NPK fertilizers do dilute other nutrients. But much of the decline is attributed to higher-yielding crop varieties with lower mineral concentrations. Fertilizers more often cure trace deficiencies than cause them. Zinc, copper, manganese, iron and molybdenum shortages found in Western Australia in the 1940s and 1950s are now corrected routinely.

soil-fert-048.title: Biofertilizers: living microbes as plant food
soil-fert-048.text: Some fertilizers are alive. A biofertilizer contains living microorganisms that colonize the {{ref:soil-bio-143}} or the plant's interior and promote growth by increasing the supply or availability of nutrients. They add nutrients by fixing nitrogen and dissolving phosphorus. Plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria and mycorrhizae make inorganic phosphorus soluble, raise mineral bioavailability and produce hormones such as auxins and gibberellin. The microbes also restore the soil's natural nutrient cycle and build organic matter. They suppress plant pathogens, protect against drought and other stresses, and detoxify pollutants below ground. Reported yield increases reach about 10–40%. Effects vary between and even within environments, and are most marked in drier climates. Biofertilizers can reduce synthetic fertilizer and pesticide use but cannot yet replace them. Compost-based inoculants serve too, including those made from {{ref:soil-fert-035}} and {{ref:soil-fert-039}}.

soil-fert-024.title: Animal manure, from farmyard straw to liquid slurry
soil-fert-024.text: Not all dung is equal. Animal manure comes from livestock dung and urine, handled either as farmyard manure or as liquid slurry. Farmyard manure includes straw bedding that has soaked up feces and urine. Slurry comes from intensive units that use concrete or slats instead of straw. Manures from horses, cattle, pigs, sheep and poultry, and guano from seabirds and bats, differ in quality and need different application rates. Sheep manure is high in nitrogen and potash, and pig manure relatively low in both. Cattle manure supplies nitrogen and organic carbon; chicken litter is rich in nitrogen and phosphate. Fresh poultry droppings harm plants but become valuable fertilizer after composting. Horse manure can carry grass and weed seeds, because horses do not digest seeds as cattle do. Manure improves soil aggregation, so the soil holds more water and nutrients. Strong-smelling slurries, such as those from intensive pig farms, are usually injected into the soil to limit odor.

soil-fert-075.title: Rock flour, ground stone that feeds the soil
soil-fert-075.text: Glaciers grinding over bedrock leave behind rock flour: fine, silt-sized rock particles. Artificial grinding gives a similar powder. The particles are ground quartz and feldspar, not clay minerals, and wind can carry them far to form loess. As rock dust, it serves organic growers as a soil conditioner that supplies micronutrients. Basalt and granite are richest, while limestone is often deficient. A 2022 study found basalt dust raised available phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium within months. Nutrient-poor soils may need 10 to 50 tonnes per hectare. The German miller Julius Hensel reported success with stonemeal in the 1890s.

soil-fert-079.title: Marl, the clay-and-carbonate earth of lakes and fens
soil-fert-079.text: Marl is an earthy material rich in carbonate minerals, clay and silt. It typically holds 35–65% clay and 65–35% carbonate, mostly calcite, and hardens into marlstone. It forms in marine or fresh water, often through algae. Marl lakes in recently glaciated areas, and very rich fens, deposit it from calcium-rich water. Farmers use it as a soil conditioner and to neutralize acid soil, adding calcium, improving structure and making other nutrients more available. Because its carbonate is mostly calcium carbonate, crops on marl-treated land may show magnesium deficiency unless magnesium is also supplied.

soil-fert-039.title: Vermicompost, compost made by worms
soil-fert-039.text: Worm castings can hold 10 to 20 times more microbial activity than the soil and organic matter the worm eats. Vermicompost is the product of composting with worms: a mix of decomposing food or plant waste, bedding and worm castings, or vermicast. The usual workers are red wigglers, Eisenia fetida or E. andrei. Composting worms are surface-dwelling epigeic species; burrowing anecic Lumbricus species adapt poorly to shallow bins. Redworms feed fastest at 15–25 °C, survive 10 °C and may be harmed above 30 °C. Bin moisture must stay above 50%, ideally 70–80%. The method treats wastes faster than conventional composting. Castings hold fewer contaminants and more concentrated nutrients than the original materials, and the worm mucus coating them slows nutrient release so nutrients do not wash away. Vermicompost can be mixed into soil or steeped as worm tea. The leachate draining from bins is different: uncomposted, it may carry pathogens.

soil-fert-022.title: Controlled-release fertilizer feeds crops slowly on purpose
soil-fert-022.text: On average, 16% of conventional nitrogen fertilizer escapes as ammonia, nitrous oxide or nitrogen gas, or washes away. Controlled-release fertilizer aims to waste less. It is a granulated fertilizer, usually supplying nitrogen, that releases its nutrients into the soil gradually over a controlled period. Ordinary fertilizers dissolve and disperse, but these are not water-soluble. Their release rate depends on low solubility in soil moisture, the breakdown of pellet coatings, and conversion of the chemicals into ammonia or another usable nutrient. Most slow-release types are urea derivatives, such as urea-formaldehyde, first made in 1936 and sold from 1955. Coated types wrap ordinary fertilizer in sulfur or plastic. Sulfur-coated urea releases as microbes degrade the sealant and through cracks, typically over 6 to 16 weeks in turf. Slow release protects crops from damage by excess fertilizer, needs fewer applications, and in most cases improves yield by more than 10%. It can also cut nitrogen pollution and nitrous oxide emissions, which arise when microbes act on ammonia faster than plants absorb it.

soil-fert-054.title: Biochar in the field: big promise, uneven results
soil-fert-054.text: Biochar does the most for degraded tropical and nutrient-poor soils, and less in temperate regions. Farmers mix it into the soil or spread it on top to raise fertility, hold water and nutrients, and store carbon over the medium to long term. Its pores and high specific surface area make it hygroscopic, so it keeps water and dissolved nutrients in the upper soil and lowers fertilizer needs. Modest additions cut nitrous oxide emissions by up to 80% and eliminate methane emissions. It can reduce leaching of E. coli through sandy soils and remove heavy metals. Soil biologist Elaine Ingham stressed its value as habitat for beneficial microbes. The drawbacks are real. Significant yield gains appear to need 2.5–20 tonnes per hectare, a cost often prohibitive for low-input field crops. Its strong adsorption can weaken pesticides, especially with high-surface-area biochars. Results depend on the biochar, the dose, the soil, temperature and humidity, and the mechanisms are still poorly understood.

soil-fert-053.title: Biochar carbon removal: locking carbon underground
soil-fert-053.text: Making biochar releases CO2, up to 50% of the biomass. The carbon left behind, though, is stable and can stay in the ground for hundreds to thousands of years. Biochar carbon removal locks carbon away on the strength of that stability. The World Bank says biochar keeps 10–70% of the original biomass carbon, about 50% on average, and slows its decomposition by one or two orders of magnitude. Charcoal-rich black spots in Belgian arable soils, left by kilns before 1870, show lower respiration and slower carbon turnover. Biochar set into concrete and tar counts too. How much it can remove is disputed. A 2021 review put the potential at 1.6–3.2 billion tonnes of CO2 a year, with roughly 0.3–1.8 Gt economically feasible below US$100 a tonne. Actual production is a few hundred thousand tonnes a year, giving well under 1 Mt CO2 of certified removal. A 2018 study doubted enough biomass exists, and some authors warn of a boom and bust.

soil-fert-084.title: How urea's nitrogen escapes into the air
soil-fert-084.text: Spread urea on dry ground, and up to thirty percent of its available nitrogen can vanish into the air within seventy-two hours. This loss of fertilizer nitrogen as ammonia gas, when urea breaks down at the soil surface, is ammonia volatilization. It starts with an enzyme. Urease hydrolyzes urea to unstable carbamic acid, which breaks down without enzymes into ammonia and carbon dioxide. The ammonia escapes unless it reacts with water to form ammonium, which plants can use and ammonia cannot. The reaction also makes hydroxide, raising the pH near each urea particle to around 9.0. That speeds volatilization and makes the zone toxic for several hours. Losses rise with temperature, pH and drying soil. Urea hydrolyzed completely within two days on soils of pH about 8.2 or more, but took twice as long at pH 5.2. Surface residues and organic-rich soils carry more urease, so they lose more. About 0.1 inch of rain soon after application moves urea into the soil. Incorporating or injecting it also reduces losses, because good soil contact buffers pH and slows ammonia formation. The stakes are high, since urea makes up more than fifty percent of the world's nitrogen fertilizers.

soil-fert-030.title: The crew that turns waste into compost
soil-fert-030.text: Bacteria do most of the work in a compost heap. They are the most abundant of the compost organisms, which range from chemical decomposers such as bacteria and fungi to physical ones such as worms and insects. Bacteria excrete plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus and magnesium. Moderate-temperature mesophilic or heat-loving thermophilic kinds dominate depending on the phase. Thermophiles, inactive between −5 and 25 °C, wake once mesophiles warm the heap and thrive at 40–60 °C. Actinomycetota break down tough paper, bark, lignin and cellulose, and fungi handle woody material bacteria cannot. Earthworms eat partly composted material, and their castings free nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium.

soil-fert-035.title: Compost tea, a brew of microbes for crops
soil-fert-035.text: Compost tea is a liquid of fermented water extracts leached from composted materials and applied to crops. It is usually made by adding compost to water at 1:4–1:10 and stirring occasionally to release microbes, with or without aeration. Field studies show benefits from its organic matter, nutrients and microbial activity, and from suppressing plant pathogens and soil-borne diseases. Aerated tea brews faster with more microbes and suppresses pathogens better than unbrewed compost extracts. Non-aerated tea is cheaper, but studies conflict on its phytotoxicity and pathogen risks. Its added nutrients can let E. coli and Salmonella regrow. Whether aeration is worth it remains debated.

soil-fert-036.title: Composting at industrial scale
soil-fert-036.text: Large-scale composting relies on three main methods. In-vessel composting confines material in tanks or bunkers where airflow and temperature are controlled, as in a bioreactor. It treats sewage sludge, food waste and municipal organics, sanitizing pathogens so the waste can be reclaimed as a soil amendment, while limiting odors, emissions and polluted water. Aerated static piles stay aerobic by forcing air through perforated pipes instead of turning, and roofs reduce leachate. Windrow composting piles manure, leftover crop material and other wastes in long rows. Such large operations can get hot enough to kill beneficial microbes while pasteurizing the waste.

soil-fert-031.title: The rise and fall of a compost heap's temperature
soil-fert-031.text: Under ideal conditions, a compost heap passes through a fixed sequence of temperature stages. In the first, mesophilic phase, microorganisms decompose the material at moderate temperatures. As the heap warms, thermophilic bacteria take over at 50 to 60 °C (122 to 140 °F). When high-energy compounds run out, the temperature falls through a cooling and a maturation phase. Mesophilic bacteria then cure the compost, making it more bioavailable to plants. Semicomposting, of volumes too small for full composting, never reaches the thermophilic stage.

soil-fert-032.title: Hot compost in weeks, cold compost in a year
soil-fert-032.text: A home heap can take up to a year to finish; a well-run hot pile, 18 days. Hot and cold composting differ in pile size and temperature, and so in how long they take. Time depends on volume, particle size, and how much the material is mixed and aerated. In hot composting, usual on municipal and farm sites, large piles reach high temperatures and stay thermophilic for days or weeks. The Berkeley method finishes in 18 days. It needs at least 1 cubic meter of material, turned every two days after the first four, with C:N at 30:1 or less. Cold composting in piles under 1 cubic meter, like most home heaps, needs no turning, but parts may go anaerobic.

soil-fert-033.title: How a compost heap's heat kills germs
soil-fert-033.text: Stabilized compost that has reached 50–70 °C poses very little risk. Those temperatures kill pathogens and weed seeds, and even make oocysts unviable. The lethal temperature depends on the organism, on how long the heat lasts, from seconds to weeks, and on pH. Finished compost also fights plant disease. Compost teas and extracts inhibit crop pathogens such as Fusarium oxysporum, Rhizoctonia and Pythium, and compost supplies biocontrol agents such as Bacillus subtilis. Sterilizing compost weakens this effect. Compost that has not passed 50 °C should be turned wearing a respirator and gloves, against aspergillosis, farmer's lung, Legionnaires' disease and tetanus.

soil-fert-081.title: Seaweed, a fertilizer from the shore
soil-fert-081.text: Brown seaweeds are the most used source of seaweed fertilizer, an organic fertilizer that raises soil fertility and plant growth. Seaweed may be laid as mulch, composted, dried and powdered, or made into liquid extracts. It supplies macro- and micronutrients, humic acids and plant hormones, and can raise crop tolerance of low moisture, high salinity and freezing. As a {{ref:soil-fert-063}}, its humic acid and soluble alginates give clay soils short of organic matter better texture, aeration and water retention. There are drawbacks. Heavy metals accumulated by seaweed may pass into crops, and the spread of diseases and invasive species is another challenge.

soil-fert-082.title: Fertilizer burn: when plant food parches a plant
soil-fert-082.text: Fertilizer burn is damage caused by too much fertilizer, the wrong type, or too little water applied with it. Excess salt, nitrogen or ammonia impairs photosynthesis and respiration, causing visible burns. When salts outside the root exceed those inside, water stops entering and may even leave the roots, so the plant responds as if in drought. Early signs are white salt marks and crusts around the roots. Later the leaves brown and die, root growth stops and roots may rot. Dry, overheated plants suffer most. Heavy watering washes the salts away; otherwise the roots are cleaned and the plant repotted.

soil-fert-086.title: Raised beds: soil that nobody walks on
soil-fert-086.text: Because no one walks on a raised bed, its soil is not compacted and roots grow easily. Raised-bed gardening means growing in soil raised above ground level, usually enclosed in a frame. The soil is usually enriched with compost. Crops are planted so close that their touching leaves suppress weeds and conserve moisture. Beds also extend the season and avoid poor native soil. Built along contour lines on slopes, they help control erosion and conserve water and nutrients. Gardeners on heavy red clay Ultisols use raised beds, or {{ref:soil-fert-088}}, to avoid amending the soil.

soil-fert-088.title: Hügelkultur, a garden bed built on rotting wood
soil-fert-088.text: Hügelkultur plants a raised bed on a mound of decaying wood and other compostable plant matter. The term was first published in a 1962 German gardening booklet by Herrman Andrä. Advocates claim it improves fertility, water retention and soil warming. Wood has one of the highest carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, so its decay may tie up soil nitrogen at first, lowering fertility for perhaps one to two years. Peer-reviewed studies are few, though a student thesis found hügel mounds held almost twice as much water as flat control plots. Advocates rely largely on personal experience. Critics say the method lacks genuine scientific principles. It also runs counter to soil building by litterfall, since in nature wood decays at the surface.
